question_text: A 52-year-old retired professional cyclist, who still rides his bike 400 miles per week, comes to his physician complaining of hand problems. explanation:
The ulnar nerve can become compressed between the pisiform and hook of the hamate at the wrist in a condition termed "ulnar canal syndrome" or "Guyon tunnel syndrome". This entrapment syndrome is especially seen in professional cyclists who spend countless hours placing pressure on the hook of the hamate bone as they grasp their handlebars. question_text: A 56-year-old woman was stopped at a light when her car was rear-ended by another car. She had her right arm on the steering wheel, and the impact caused forced flexion at her elbow. Several months later, she comes to her physician complaining of numbness and a "pins and needles" sensation in her right little finger when she talks on the phone, rests her head on her right hand at work, or spends most of her day typing at work. She also notices the quality of her typing and her ability to play the violin have diminished. Which nerve is compressed at what location?
explanation:
Situations in which peripheral nerves are compressed or otherwise entrapped where they pass through narrow spaces ("tunnels") in muscles and/or osseo-fascial units are generally referred to as "tunnel syndromes". Such conditions may result in periodic or constant motor and/or sensory deficits. The ulnar nerve crosses the elbow in a narrow space between the olecranon process and the medial epicondyle of the humerus, on the posteromedial (ulnar) side of the joint. The ulnar nerve can be compressed between these bony landmarks or between the humeral and ulnar heads of the attachment of the flexor carpi ulnaris. Compression of the ulnar nerve within these areas leads to "cubital tunnel syndrome". The symptoms are exacerbated during events where flexion of the elbow narrows these passageways and compresses the ulnar nerve at the elbow joint. The patient's cubital tunnel syndrome would explain the paresthesia and numbness on the medial aspect of the hand and the diminished fine motor control of the intrinsic hand muscles. Her condition originated due to the forced flexion of the elbow in the motor vehicle accident, which compressed the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel.

question_text: After a fall from a height with his hand outstretched, a man is brought to the emergency department. An X-ray reveals a fracture in the clavicle. Which specific region of the clavicle is the most likely to be fractured?
explanation:
Explanation:

The junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third is the most common site for clavicular fractures.(Option B,C and D ruled out).

This region represents a transitional zone between the rigidly supported medial segment (by sternoclavicular ligaments) and the more mobile lateral segment, making it biomechanically weak and susceptible to fractures from indirect forces like a fall on an outstretched hand.

  • Location & Shape: A long, slightly S-shaped bone positioned horizontally at the neck-trunk junction.
  • Articulations:
    • Medially: With the sternum and first rib cartilage.
    • Laterally: With the acromion process of the scapula.
  • Key Structural Features:
    • The only long bone that lies horizontally.
    • It is subcutaneous (easily felt under the skin) along its entire length.
    • It lacks a medullary (bone marrow) cavity.
  • Ossification (Bone Formation):
    • First bone to begin ossifying (5th-6th week of fetal development).
    • Last bone to complete ossification (around age 25).
    • The only long bone with two primary ossification centers.
    • Ossifies primarily in membrane (intramembranous ossification), with the exception of its medial end, which ossifies in cartilage (endochondral ossification).

Key Takeaways:

  • The most common clavicle fracture site is the junction of the middle and lateral thirds.
  • This is often caused by a fall onto the shoulder or an outstretched hand.

question_text: Incudomalleolar joint is which of the following type of joint?
option_c: Ball and socket variety of synovial joint
explanation:
Explanation:

The incudomalleolar joint (between the malleus and incus) is a saddle-type synovial joint, where each articular surface is concave in one direction and convex in the other.

Saddle (Sellar) joints:

  • Articular surfaces are reciprocally
  • Following free movements are permitted:
    • Flexion and extension around the transverse axis.
    • Abduction and adduction around the anteroposterior axis.
    • Combination of movements produces circumduction.
    • Conjunct rotation occurs around a third axis; however, cannot occur independently.

Plane variety of synovial joint (Option A):
Plane joints have flat articular surfaces that permit simple gliding movements, such as in intercarpal joints. The incudomalleolar joint, however, has reciprocally concavo-convex surfaces, not flat surfaces, making this classification incorrect.

Ball and socket variety of synovial joint (Option C):
Ball and socket joints, like the hip and shoulder, allow multiaxial movement including flexion, extension, rotation, and circumduction. The incudomalleolar joint does not have a spherical head articulating with a cup-shaped socket, nor does it permit such wide ranges of motion.

Condylar variety of synovial joint (Option D):
Condylar joints allow biaxial movement, such as flexion-extension and side-to-side motions, seen in the metacarpophalangeal joints. The incudomalleolar joint does not have oval condyles articulating with corresponding depressions, and its movement range is much more limited.

Key takeaways:

  • Articular surfaces of saddle joints are reciprocally concavo-convex,
  • Examples:
    • First carpometacarpal joint
    • Sternoclavicular joint
    • Calcaneocuboid joint
    • Incudomalleolar joint

  • Posterior terminal branch - provides motor innervation to the posterior aspect of the deltoid muscle and teres minor. It also innervates the skin over the inferior part of the deltoid as the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
  • Anterior terminal branch - winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and provides motor innervation to the anterior aspect of the deltoid muscle. It terminates with cutaneous branches to the anterior and anterolateral shoulder.
  • Articular branch - supplies the glenohumeral joint

question_text: A middle-aged woman comes to you complaining of pain on the lateral side of her right elbow, so severe that she holds her eating utensils in her left hand to eat. She says that she spent the weekend putting in a new garden plot and that it involved loosening and turning over a large area of grass sods with a garden fork. You find that the region just proximal to the lateral epicondyle of her humerus is painful to the touch. There is no sensory loss in her forearm or hand. You suspect a localized tearing of the origin of a muscle producing the equivalent of condition shown below. The muscle most likely involved is the:
explanation:
Tennis elbow is usually caused by inflammation of the common extensor tendon on the lateral side of the forearm, but we know that that's not what happened here. Instead, the patient tore a muscle at its origin, near the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. Brachioradialis originates from the upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, so this is the muscle that she probably tore. This also makes sense given her activities brachioradialis flexes the elbow and assists in pronation and supination, so she would have been using this muscle while gardening.

The common flexor tendon is associated with the medial epicondyle, not the lateral epicondyle. Extensor carpi radialis brevis and extensor digitorum take origin from the common extensor tendon, which attaches to the lateral epicondyle. This tendon would be inflamed in a classic case of tennis elbow, but the common extensor tendon is not the structure that was injured in this patient's case. Pronator teres takes origin from the common flexor tendon and the medial side of the ulna.

question_text: Upon finding a malignant tumor in the medial portion of the breast of a 40-year-old female, the surgeon began to search for the lymph nodes that would be the first ones reached by metastatic spread of cancer cells from this site. Which group(s) would have to be examined to determine whether metastasis had occurred?
explanation:
As lymph drains from the breast, the majority of fluid travels to two groups of lymph nodes: the axillary and the parasternal. 75% of the lymph goes to the axillary lymph nodes, with the pectoral nodes being the first axillary nodes to receive the drainage. So, the pectoral nodes would need to be inspected to determine whether cancer had spread to the axillary system. Central and apical nodes are also part of the axillary system. These nodes might receive cancerous cells, but they are more distal sites of drainage. Cancer would be most likely to metastasize to the pectoral nodes first.

The parasternal nodes receive most of the lymph that does not drain into the axillary nodes. They are an especially important route of drainage from the medial side of the breast. So, it is also important to survey these nodes to determine whether cancer has spread into the lymphatics.

question_text: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Pivot joints enable rotational movements like supination and pronation.

question_text: The signs and symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome may vary among patients, but they always result from compression of what structure in the carpal canal?
explanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by a compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. The carpal tunnel is a canal on the anterior side of the wrist. It is made of the carpal bones which are covered by the flexor retinaculum. It contains the tendon of flexor pollicis longus, the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, and the median nerve. If the sheath over the common flexor tendons, the ulnar bursa, becomes inflamed, this can compress the median nerve in the canal, leading to pain and weakness in the hand. None of the other structures mentioned in the question are contained in the carpal tunnel, so they would not be compressed in that space.

question_text: A 45-year-old diabetic worker sustains a stab injury to the central region of his palm. question_text: A person riding a mountain bike on a rustic trail hits a rut, the fork of the bike breaks and the person is thrown into a tree, severely fracturing the upper end of his humerus. question_text: The tendons on the dorsal side of the wrist are held in place by a thickening of the antebrachial fascia called the:

question_text: The emphysema is characterised by:
option_a: Over secretion of mucous in the bronchus
option_c: Enlarged alveoli with destruction of interalveolar septum
option_d: Widen and thickened wall of the bronchi
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Emphysema is a condition of the lung characterized by permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole.
  • This enlargement is accompanied by destruction of the alveolar wall.
  • Thus, significant surface area for gas exchange is lost in this disease.
  • It is caused by impairment of synthesis of elastic fibres and other components of septum.
  • Emphysema is often caused by chronic inhalations of foreign particulate material, such as coal dust, textile fibers, and construction dust.
  • The most common cause, however, is cigarette smoking.
  • Over secretion of mucous in the bronchus (Option A): True for chronic bronchitis, not emphysema.
  • Spasmodic narrowing of the bronchi (Option B): Characteristic of bronchial asthma, not emphysema.
  • Widen and thickened wall of the bronchi (Option D): Related to bronchiectasis, not emphysema.

Key Takeaways:

  • Emphysema is characterized by enlarged alveoli and destruction of interalveolar septa due to loss of elastic tissue.
  • Chronic bronchitis involves overproduction of mucus, while bronchial asthma is marked by spasmodic airway narrowing.

question_text: A 50-year-old diabetic woman comes in with a 6-week history of burning pain and numbness in her hand, particularly disturbing her at night.   • The symptoms of burning discomfort, nighttime paresthesias, sensory loss in the lateral 3½ digits, and atrophy of the thenar muscles strongly point toward a median nerve entrapment at the wrist.

Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when the space within the carpal tunnel becomes narrowed or when its contents (mainly the flexor tendons) swell, leading to pressure on the median nerve.

  • Diabetes (as in this patient)
  • Tenosynovitis of flexor tendons
  • Myxoedema
  • Pregnancy-related fluid retention
  • Fracture or dislocation of the lunate bone

Typical clinical features:

  • Burning or tingling sensation in the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger
  • Symptoms worsening at night
  • Weakness of thumb opposition and grip
  • Thenar muscle wasting in long-standing cases
  • Possible "ape-thumb" posture from loss of thumb opposition

Cubital tunnel syndrome (Option A): Compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow; causes numbness in the medial 1½ fingers, not the lateral 3½.

De Quervain's disease (Option B): Inflammation of tendons at the radial wrist (APL and EPB); causes wrist pain, not median nerve symptoms.

Guyon canal syndrome (Option D): Ulnar nerve compression at the wrist; affects medial digits, not thenar muscles

question_text: A girl playing softball cuts the palm of her hand as she scoops up a piece of glass along with the ball. If the only nerve damaged is the recurrent branch of the median nerve, she would lose what movement of the thumb?
explanation:
If the recurrent branch of the median nerve was injured, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis would be denervated. Opponens is the only muscle that allows for opposition of the thumb. So, by denervating opponens, the girl would no longer be able to oppose her thumb. Although abductor pollicis brevis would be denervated, abductor pollicis longus would still be functional, so she could abduct her thumb. Adductor pollicis is in the adductor/interosseous compartment, deep in the center of the hand, and it is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This means that adduction would not be affected by the injury to the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Although flexor pollicis brevis was denervated, this is not the flexor that is responsible for flexion at the distal phalanx. Flexor pollicis longus controls flexion at the distal phalanx, and it is a muscle of the forearm which is innervated by the median nerve.

question_text: What arterial vessel accompanies the deep branch of the ulnar nerve across the palm?
explanation:
The deep palmar arterial arch is made by the radial artery and the deep branch of the ulnar artery. It runs deep in the hand, along with the deep ulnar nerve which innervates the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Although the radial artery contributes to the deep palmar arterial arch, it does not run with the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Radialis indicis is a branch of the radial artery that runs up the radial side of the index finger, similar to a proper digital artery. The superficial palmar arterial arch is made of the ulnar artery and a superficial branch of the radial artery. question_text: A 10-year-old boy was running across a parking lot when he tripped and received lacerations on the base of his thumb from a broken glass bottle. On examination, his thumb was unable to oppose to his fingers, and the thumb also showed weakness when abducting and flexing. No sensory deficits were reported. What nerve was most likely severed?
explanation:
The recurrent (thenar) branch of the median nerve lies subcutaneously in the thenar eminence and can be damaged by lacerations in this area. This nerve innervates most of the thenar muscles, including the Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, and superficial head of the Flexor pollicis brevis (mnemonic = "OAF"). Opposition of the thumb would be lost by cutting the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Though the abductor pollicis brevis is denervated, the abductor pollicis longus, innervated by the deep branch of the radial nerve, is still intact. Also, the flexor pollicis longus, innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve, would still allow flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb. Cutting the recurrent branch of the median nerve would lead to atrophy of the thenar muscular complex, a condition known as "ape hand".

question_text: A boy fell onto a sharp object and cut his deep radial nerve as it emerged from the supinator muscle. The artery joining it at this point was also injured. The injured artery is the:

The ulnar and radial arteries are branches of the brachial artery that run down the ulnar and radial sides of the anterior arm.

question_text: As part of a physical examination to evaluate intrinsic hand muscle function, a physician asks the patient to assume the Z-position (seen in photo) with his hand, which involves flexion of the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension of the interphalangeal joints of the fingers. Which of the following nerves is being tested in assuming this position?
explanation:
The deep branch of the ulnar nerve innervates most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including the hypothenar muscles, medial two lumbrical muscles, the palmar and dorsal interossei, adductor pollicis, and the deep head of the flexor pollicis brevis. Specifically, the palmar interossei, dorsal interossei, and lumbrical muscles insert into the extensor digital expansion to provide, collectively, flexion of the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension of the interphalangeal joints of the fingers.

All of these muscles, with the exception of the first and second lumbrical muscles, are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, so this nerve is being tested by placing the hand in the Z-position. If the deep branch of the ulnar nerve were severed, the hand would assume the opposite of the Z-position, which is called "claw hand."

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 816

question_text: After suffering a gunshot wound to the forearm, it was determined that the posterior interosseous nerve was severed. What function was lost?
option_c: Motor to the extensor carpi radialis longus
option_d: Parasympathetic to the dorsum of the forearm
explanation:
The posterior interosseous nerve is the sensory continuation of the deep radial nerve, distal to its motor branches for the extensor muscles. It reaches the wrist joint and carpal bones for proprioceptive sense from these structures. Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus are innervated by the radial nerve, and extensor carpi radialis brevis is innervated by the deep radial nerve. Flexor digitorum superficialis is innervated by the median nerve. There are no parasympathetic nerves in the limbs or body wall.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 818

question_text: In order to evaluate the carpal-metacarpal joint of the thumb, the median nerve must be deadened at the wrist (causing paralysis of the muscles supplied by it distal to the injection) to test the joint. Which movement of the thumb would be most affected by the anesthetic?
explanation:
If the median nerve was deadened at the wrist, a patient would lose the use of the thenar compartment of the hand. Abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis would be paralyzed. Opponens is the only muscle that allows for opposition of the thumb, so a patient would no longer be able to oppose the thumb to the fingers. Although abductor pollicis brevis would be paralyzed, abductor pollicis longus would still be functional and the patient could still abduct the thumb. Adductor pollicis is in the adductor compartment, and it is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This means that adduction would not be affected by deadening the median nerve. Extensor pollicis brevis and longus are innervated by the deep radial nerve, so extension would still be intact. Although flexor pollicis brevis would be denervated, flexor pollicis longus could still flex the thumb. It is a muscle of the forearm which is innervated by the median nerve proximal to the site of the anesthesia.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 763

question_text: In carpal tunnel syndrome, compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel affects which hand muscle?
explanation:
The recurrent branch of the median nerve innervates the thenar compartment, including abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis. If the median nerve was damaged, any of these muscles might be denervated. Adductor pollicis, the palmar interosseous muscles, and opponens digiti minimi are all innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

question_text: A 21-year-old male college student reports to the student health clinic on Monday morning, the day after the Super Bowl. He explains that he was intoxicated and lost consciousness with his upper limbs draped over the back of a couch. He complains of numbness and paresthesia over the dorsum of his hand on the radial side and is unable to support the weight of his left hand when the hand is placed in a pronated position (see photo), What nerve was most likely damaged in this
explanation:
This case represents a classic presentation of "Saturday Night Palsy", where the radial nerve is compressed against the humerus in the arm. Remember, the radial nerve supplies motor innervation to the posterior compartments of the arm and forearm, so damage to this nerve would cause weakness in extending the elbow and wrist. This patient is unable to extend the wrist when the hand is placed in a pronated position ("wrist drop"), implying damage to the radial nerve. Moreover, the superficial branch of the radial nerve is responsible for cutaneous innervation over much of the dorsum of the hand, which explains the numbness and paresthesia in his hand.

question_text: During a motorcycle accident, an 18-year-old male landed on the right lateral side of his rib cage with his right upper limb abducted. In the hospital he was found to have "winging" of the right scapula. Which nerve was likely damaged in the accident?
explanation:
An injury to the long thoracic nerve denervates serratus anterior, meaning that there will be no muscle protracting the scapula and counteracting trapezius and the rhomboids, powerful retractors of the scapula. This means that the scapula will be winged backwards, which is this patient's main symptom. The long thoracic nerve is derived from the nerve roots of C5-7. This nerve is particularly vulnerable to iatrogenic injury during surgical procedures, such as mastectomies, because it is located on the superficial side of serratus anterior.

The accessory nerve innervates trapezius an injury to this nerve might lead to an inability to raise the acromion of the shoulder. The lateral pectoral nerve is a small nerve that provides innervation to pectoralis major. The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm. The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the thorax and much of the abdominal viscera. The patient's symptoms do not fit with an injury to any of these nerves.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 829

question_text: A 45-year-old woman who underwent breast cancer surgery one month ago now presents with a noticeable bony prominence on the left side of her back. On examination, the medial border of her left scapula is markedly prominent, and this prominence becomes more obvious when she pushes against a wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A prominent medial border of the scapula that becomes more noticeable when the patient pushes against resistance is classic for winging of the scapula.
  • This occurs due to injury of the long thoracic nerve, which supplies the serratus anterior muscle.
  • Breast surgeries (especially axillary lymph node dissection) place this nerve at risk.

Winging of scapula:

  • Caused by paralysis of the serratus anterior
  • Due to injury of the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7)
  • The scapula lifts off the thoracic wall, especially along the medial border
  • Worsens when the patient performs a wall push test
  • Common after breast cancer surgery, trauma, or axillary node dissection

Functional features:

  • Difficulty raising the arm above the head
  • Weak protraction of the scapula
  • Medial border of scapula becomes prominent

Erb's paralysis (Option B): Upper brachial plexus injury (C5-C6); presents with "waiter's tip" deformity, not scapular winging.

Klumpke's paralysis (Option C): Lower brachial plexus injury (C8-T1); presents with claw hand, not scapular prominence.

Trapezius paralysis (Option D): Due to spinal accessory nerve injury; causes lateral scapular winging, but the medial border prominence seen here is typical of serratus anterior paralysis.

question_text: A patient develops a deformity as shown following overhead weight-lifting exercises. Which muscle is most likely involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a prominent protrusion of the medial border of the scapula, known as winging of the scapula. This finding is most likely due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, resulting from injury to the long thoracic nerve.

Serratus Anterior Muscle

  • The Serratus Anterior muscle is located on the lateral aspect of the thorax.
  • Origin:Upper 8 ribs (anterolateral surface).
  • Insertion:Costal (anterior) surface of scapula.
  • Nerve Supply:Long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).

Functions

  • Protraction of scapula (pulls scapula forward).
  • Stabilizes scapula against thoracic wall (prevents winging).
  • Lateral rotation of the scapula: Allows glenoid cavity to turn upward, enabling full overhead abduction of the arm.

Clinical Importance

  • Injury to thelong thoracic nerve leads to paralysis of the serratus anterior.
  • Patients will present with:
    • Winging of scapula: The medial border of the scapula protrudes from the thoracic wall.
    • Inability to fully abduct arm overhead.
  • Causes:Post-mastectomy, trauma, weight-lifting injuries.

Explanation of other options:

Trapezius (Option A): Paralysis of the trapezius muscle, due to spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) injury, leads to shoulder drooping and impaired shrugging, but does not produce the classic winging of scapula.

Latissimus dorsi (Option C): The latissimus dorsi muscle, supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve, is responsible for n adduction, extension, and medial rotation of the humerus.

Supraspinatus (Option D): The supraspinatus muscle, innervated by the suprascapular nerve, initiates the first 15° of arm abduction. It does not contribute to scapular stability and is therefore not involved in scapular winging.

 

Reference:

  1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2684151/

question_text: Based on the clinical image below, what is the most probable nerve to be injured?
explanation:
Explanation :

The image shows a medial protrusion of the scapula, consistent with scapular winging. This occurs due to injury of the long thoracic nerve, which weakens the serratus anterior muscle, leading to the observed deformity.

Long thoracic nerve

  • Origin: Branches from the ventral rami of C5, C6, and C7 above the clavicle.
  • The long thoracic nerve descends vertically through the neck, passes the axillary inlet, and travels along the medial wall of the axilla to supply the serratus anterior muscle.
  • The nerve lies on the superficial aspect of serratus anterior muscle.
  • Actions of serratus anterior muscle
    • Protraction of scapula (pulls scapula forward).
    • Stabilizes scapula against thoracic wall (prevents winging).
    • Lateral rotation of the scapula: Allows the glenoid cavity to turn upward, enabling full overhead abduction of the arm.
  • Clinical significance
    • Susceptible to injury during axillary surgery, first rib operations, posterior triangle procedures, and misplaced intercostal drains.
    • Nerve injury leads to paralysis of the serratus anterior.
    • Patients will present with:
      • Winging of scapula: The medial border of the scapula protrudes from the thoracic wall.
      • Inability to fully abduct arm overhead.

Explanation of other options:

Thoracodorsal nerve (Option A): The thoracodorsal nerve, arising mainly from C7 with contributions from C6 and C8, innervates the latissimus dorsi muscle and is often used as a donor for nerve grafts in surgical procedures.

Axillary nerve (Option B): The axillary nerve, arising from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, innervates the teres minor and deltoid muscles, provides sensation to the shoulder skin, and supplies the glenohumeral joint. It is commonly injured during orthopedic surgeries, shoulder dislocations, and rotator cuff tears.

Intercostal nerve (Option D): The intercostal nerves (T1–T11) provide sensory innervation to the skin of the chest wall and abdomen, and motor innervation to the intercostal and abdominal muscles.

question_text: A 50-year-old man who has been using axillary crutches for many years presents with difficulty gripping objects. On examination, he shows a complete loss of extension at the elbow, wrist, and finger joints, along with marked muscle wasting of the posterior arm and forearm. He also has sensory loss over the back of his arm, the posterior forearm, and much of the dorsum of the hand. Which nerve is most likely involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

Prolonged pressure from axillary crutches can injure the radial nerve high in the axilla, producing a classic "crutch palsy." This causes:

  • Loss of elbow extension due to paralysis of the triceps
  • Loss of wrist and finger extension (wrist drop) due to paralysis of all extensor muscles in the posterior forearm
  • Sensory loss over:
    • The posterior arm (posterior cutaneous nerve of arm)
    • The posterior forearm (posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm)
    • The lateral two-thirds of the dorsum of the hand and the lateral three and a half fingers (superficial radial nerve)

Radial nerve:

  • Largest branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus
  • Root value: C5, C6, C7, C8, T1
  • Motor supply:
    • Triceps in the arm
    • All extensor muscles at the back of the forearm (wrist and finger extensors)
  • Sensory supply:
    • Posterior arm
    • Posterior forearm
    • Lateral 2/3 of dorsum of hand
    • Lateral 3½ digits (via superficial radial nerve)

A high lesion in the axilla affects every major branch, which explains the widespread motor and sensory findings in this patient.

Ulnar Nerve (Option B): Causes intrinsic hand muscle weakness and clawing; elbow and wrist extension remain normal.

Median Nerve (Option C): Affects thumb opposition and lateral digits; wrist extension preserved.

Anterior interosseous Nerve (Option D): Pure motor branch of the median nerve; no sensory loss and no effect on elbow/wrist extension.

question_text: A patient came with numbness and shooting pain along the medial aspect of the forearm, also including the medial half of the fourth and the fifth digits. Which syndrome would you diagnose?
explanation:
Cubital tunnel syndrome is a neuropathy of the ulnar nerve causing symptoms of numbness and shooting pain along the medial aspect of the forearm, also including the medial half of the fourth digit and the fifth digit. It is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow region.

question_text: A 42-year-old man broke a window with his fist to rescue his child from a house fire. The man sustained a laceration to the lateral aspect of his right forearm, but he only showed a sensory deficit (numbness and paresthesia) to the dorsolateral aspect of his hand (as denoted by the shaded area within the given photo). What nerve was most likely damaged?
option_a: Dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve
option_b: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm

This nerve is vulnerable as it runs posteriorly between the brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus tendons toward the dorsum of the hand. This nerve was damaged at this location, but the area of sensory loss is less than expected due to the overlap from cutaneous branches of the ulnar and median nerves.

Axillary artery:

  • The axillary artery is closely related to the divisions of the brachial plexus deep to the clavicle, and to the cords below it.

question_text: What movement of the thumb would be most affected by lesion of the median nerve in the cubital fossa:
explanation:
If the median nerve was injured in the cubital fossa, all the muscles innervated by the median nerve which are found distal to the cubital fossa would be injured. The thenar compartment of the hand and the flexor muscles of the forearm would be denervated (with the exception of flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus both of these muscles are innervated by the ulnar nerve). This means that none of the muscles which allow for flexion of the thumb would be intact. Flexor pollicis brevis is innervated by the recurrent branch of the median nerve and flexor pollicis longus is innervated by the median nerve. Both of these muscles would be denervated. Abduction is performed by abductor pollicis longus (innervated by the radial nerve) and abductor pollicis brevis (innervated by the median nerve). So, abduction might be weakened, but it would not be completely lost following damage to the median nerve. Adduction is performed by adductor pollicis, which is a muscle in the medial compartment of the hand, innervated by the deep ulnar nerve. Extending the thumb is accomplished by extensor pollicis longus and brevis, which are both innervated by the deep radial nerve.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 818

question_text: A 22-year-old male patient, after an injury, presented with a deformity as shown in the image. Which nerve will be damaged in the given condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows wrist drop and is associated with a shaft of humerus fracture, indicating injury to the radial nerve.

Radial Nerve:

  • Root origin: C5-T1
  • Common causes of injury:
    • Compression in the axilla (e.g., crutch use, 'Saturday night palsy')
    • Midshaft humerus fracture
    • Repetitive pronation/supination ('screwdriver use,' finger drop)
  • Features:
    • Above elbow injury: Loss of sensation over the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsal hand; wrist drop (loss of elbow, wrist, and finger extension); decreased grip strength.
    • Below elbow injury: Distal paresthesias without wrist drop.
    • Midshaft fracture: Triceps function and posterior arm sensation are usually spared.

Explanation of other options:

Ulnar Nerve (Option A): Innervates forearm and hand muscles involved in wrist flexion and finger abduction. It is not responsible for wrist extension and, therefore, not involved in wrist drop.

Median Nerve (Option C): Supplies anterior forearm muscles and hand muscles, but does not contribute significantly to wrist extension, the primary deficit in this case.

Musculocutaneous Nerve (Option D): Innervates anterior arm muscles such as biceps brachii, which assist in elbow flexion, not wrist extension.

question_text: A 30-year-old male presents with pain and numbness in his right hand and forearm. Symptoms worsen when he lifts his arm or tilts his head to the opposite side. Chest X-ray shows a bony projection extending from the C7 vertebra. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A cervical rib is an extra rib arising from the 7th cervical vertebra (C7). It can compress the lower trunk of brachial plexus (C8-T1) or subclavian artery, producing:

  • Pain in arm and forearm
  • Numbness/tingling along ulnar distribution
  • Symptoms aggravated by raising the arm
  • Symptoms worsened by head tilt to opposite side
  • Visible bony structure on X-ray from C7

This presentation is classic for thoracic outlet syndrome due to a cervical rib.

Cervical Rib & Thoracic Outlet Syndrome:

  • Accessory rib from C7
  • Causes neurovascular compression
  • Affects:
    • Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) → Sensory loss, weakness
    • Subclavian artery → Ischemic symptoms
  • Clinical maneuvers that worsen symptoms:
    • Raising the arm
    • Neck tilt to opposite side
    • Adson test (diminished radial pulse)

Diagnosis:

  • Confirmed on X-ray showing a rib extending from C7.

Cubital tunnel syndrome (Option A): Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow.

Fracture of rib (Option B): Would show broken rib.

Carpal tunnel syndrome (Option D): Median nerve compression at wrist; does not cause radiographic cervical rib or symptoms with neck movements.

question_text: A 60-year-old female visited the emergency department after slipping and falling on an outstretched hand. She has shoulder pain and is unable to abduct her arm. Examination shows swelling and tenderness over the proximal humerus. X-ray reveals a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. Which of the following statements is true for the injured nerve?
option_a: It is the branch of medial cord of brachial plexus
option_b: It passes through quadrangular space along with posterior circumflex artery
option_d: It provides sensory innervations to skin over medial side of arm and forearm
explanation:
Explanation:

A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus commonly injures the axillary nerve. The axillary nerve travels through quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.

Axillary Nerve (C5-C6)

  • Origin: Posterior cord of brachial plexus
  • Course:
    • Winds around the surgical neck of humerus
    • Passes through the quadrangular space with posterior circumflex humeral artery
  • Motor supply:
    • Deltoid is responsible for arm abduction beyond 15 degrees
    • Teres minor
  • Sensory supply:
    • Upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm (skin over lateral shoulder - regimental badge area)
  • Clinical Features of Injury:
    • Inability to abduct arm beyond 15 degrees
    • Flattening of shoulder contour
    • Sensory loss over lateral shoulder

It is the branch of medial cord (Option A): Axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord, not medial.

It supplies teres major (Option C): Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve.

It provides sensory to medial side of arm and forearm (Option D): This area is supplied by medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm. Axillary nerve supplies the lateral shoulder.

question_text: A 50-year female equestrian is thrown from a startled horse and dragged by the reins, which were wrapped around her left wrist, for some distance. At the ER, she is experiencing pain and paresthesia in the axilla and medial aspect of her upper limb. Despite being left-handed, she has marked weakness in the movements of her dominant hand, especially abduction and adduction of the fingers. What structure was most likely damaged in this woman?
option_a: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
option_b: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
option_c: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
option_d: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
explanation:
This woman has experienced a lower brachial plexus injury due to forced abduction of the upper limb during the accident. This injury presents with numbness and paresthesia in the C8 and T1 dermatomes, which supply the axilla and medial aspect of her upper limb. These nerve roots primarily supply the medial cord of the brachial plexus, which creates the ulnar nerve. Due to damage to the ulnar nerve, she is experiencing weakness in the movement of her left hand. The abduction and adduction of the fingers are controlled by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve by supplying the dorsal interosseous and palmar interosseous muscles, respectively.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 747

question_text: Following a radical mastectomy procedure, a surgeon plans to conduct a breast reconstruction utilizing a latissimus dorsi muscle flap. What nerve will the surgeon need to keep intact during the surgical dissection of the chest wall to prevent atrophy of the muscle flap?
explanation:
Successful transposition of muscle flaps in reconstructive surgery hinges largely on maintaining the neurovascular pedicles that supply the muscle. The latissimus dorsi muscle is innervated by the thoracodorsal (middle subscapular) nerve, a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Lesion of this nerve during dissection of the chest wall will cause loss of the muscle flap.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 747

question_text: A 34-year-old male presents with medial elbow pain for 4-6 weeks, worsened by weightlifting. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial epicondyle and a positive reverse Cozen's test. Which nerve is most likely involved in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Golfer's elbow results from inflammation at the origin of the flexor tendons at the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
  • The hallmark symptom in medial epicondylitis is tenderness 5-10 mm distal to the medial epicondyle, with pain aggravated by resisted wrist flexion and pronation, as demonstrated by a positive reverse Cozen's test.

Ulnar nerve injury

    • Fracture of the hook of hamate (distal lesion), such as from a fall on an outstretched hand or compression during cycling.

    • Ulnar claw on finger extension.
    • Radial deviation of the wrist during flexion (proximal lesion).
    • Weak flexion of the ring and little fingers.
    • Loss of finger abduction and adduction (interossei paralysis).
    • Loss of thumb adduction (adductor pollicis paralysis).

Explanation of other options:

Compression or injury causes carpal tunnel syndrome, leading to pain in the anterior forearm and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers.

Radial nerve (Option C): The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) and supplies the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers. It may be injured in midshaft fractures of the humerus or axillary compression, resulting in wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.

Axillary nerve (Option D): The axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5-C6) and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. It innervates the deltoid and teres minor muscles and provides sensation over the lateral aspect of the shoulder, known as the regimental badge area. Injury to this nerve typically results in deltoid weakness, shoulder flattening, and sensory loss over the lateral shoulder.

question_text: If the musculocutaneous nerve is severed at its origin from the brachial plexus, flexion at the elbow is greatly weakened but not abolished. What muscle remains operative and can contribute to flexion?

question_text: In a patient with Erb-Duchenne palsy, a nerve arising from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus is nonfunctional. This nerve is the:
explanation:
Erb-Duchenne palsy is the avulsion of the C5 and C6 roots of the brachial plexus. The suprascapular nerve comes from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus to innervate supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Since the superior trunk is made entirely from the C5 and C6 nerve roots, it makes sense that the suprascapular nerve would be damaged in Erb-Duchenne palsy. The dorsal scapular nerve comes off of the C5 root to innervate levator scapulae and the rhomboids. This nerve would also be damaged in a case of Erb-Duchenne palsy, but it is not coming off of the superior trunk. (Remember: the question specified the superior trunk!) The long thoracic nerve comes off the roots of C5, C6 and C7 to innervate serratus anterior. This nerve would be affected by Erb-Duchenne palsy, but it's not from the superior trunk. Finally, the lateral and medial pectoral nerves come off the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus, respectively. Lateral pectoral nerve would be affected in Erb's palsy, but not medial pectoral.

question_text: In a case of Erb's palsy, where roots C5 and C6 of the brachial plexus are avulsed (torn out) which muscle is paralyzed?
explanation:
The C5 and C6 roots make the superior trunk of the brachial plexus. So, all the muscles innervated by nerves from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus will be denervated following the avulsion. Supraspinatus is innervated by the suprascapular nerve, which comes off of the superior trunk of the brachial plexus. This means that avulsing the C5 and C6 nerve roots would denervate supraspinatus and paralyze that muscle.

Latissimus dorsi is innervated by the thoracodorsal nerve, which comes off the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. The thoracodorsal nerve is made of contributions from C6, 7, and 8 so this nerve would be mostly intact. Pectoralis minor is innervated by the medial pectoral nerve, off the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It is made of contributions from C8 and T1. Trapezius is innervated by the accessory nerve, CN XI. This means that trapezius is not innervated by the brachial plexus. Finally, triceps brachii is innervated by the radial nerve. The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, and it is made of contributions from C5, 6, 7, 8 and T1. Triceps brachi would not be entirely paralyzed following an injury to the C5 and C6 nerve roots.

question_text: A newborn delivered by difficult shoulder extraction develops weakness in the right upper limb. The given image shows the typical posture of this condition. Which nerve roots are most commonly injured?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Erb's palsy occurs due to injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, which involves the C5 and C6 nerve roots.
  • This usually happens when the head and shoulder are excessively separated during delivery or trauma.
  • As a result, nerves such as the suprascapular, axillary, and musculocutaneous are affected.
  • The muscles supplied by these nerves, including the deltoid, biceps, brachialis, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus, become paralysed.
  • Because of this, the arm hangs by the side, is medially rotated at the shoulder, the elbow is extended, and the forearm is pronated. This posture is classically described as the "waiter's tip deformity."

Explanation of other options:

C4, C5 (Option A): C4 not classically involved; upper plexus injury is limited to C5-C6.

C6, C7 (Option C): Would involve different deficits (wrist drop-like picture if the radial nerve is affected).

C8, T1 (Option D): Lower plexus injury seen in Klumpke's palsy, leading to claw hand from intrinsic muscle paralysis.

question_text: The celiac plexus of nerves may contain fibers derived from all of the following sources except:
explanation:
The celiac plexus of nerves contains fibers from the greater thoracic splanchnic nerves, which are synapsing in the celiac ganglia. This plexus also contains vagal fibers. Even though the vagus does not synapse in the celiac ganglia, it passes through the ganglia and contributes to the celiac plexus. This allows the vagal fibers to travel on arteries to reach their eventual targets. The lesser thoracic splanchnic nerves are not part of the celiac ganglia--these nerves synapse in the aorticorenal ganglia and contribute to the renal plexus. The first lumbar splanchnic nerve may occasionally contribute to the celiac plexus.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Abdomen, Page number - 186

question_text: The pelvic splanchnic nerves primarily carry ____________ to the _____________ plexus.
explanation:
Although all the other splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibers, the pelvic splanchnic nerves transmit preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from S2, 3, and 4. These fibers are carried to the inferior hypogastric plexus. The parasympathetic fibers from the inferior hypogastric plexus supply the smooth muscle of the pelvic viscera, while the sympathetic fibers from the inferior hypogastric plexus supply vascular smooth muscle of vessels supplying the pelvic viscera. The superior hypogastric plexus is a continuation of the intermesenteric plexus it contributes sympathetic fibers to the inferior hypogastric plexus through hypogastric nerves.

question_text: During a neurological examination, the doctor asks a patient to hold a piece of paper between two adjacent fingers while the doctor tries to pull it away. Which nerve is being tested?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The ability to grip a sheet of paper between two fingers depends on the palmar interossei muscles, which are responsible for adduction of the fingers.
  • These muscles are supplied entirely by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. I
  • f the ulnar nerve is weak or injured, the patient will not be able to hold the paper firmly; it is indicative of a positive paper-pull (card) test.

The ulnar nerve is the primary motor nerve of the hand. After entering the palm superficial to the flexor retinaculum, it divides into a superficial and a deep branch.

Superficial branch supplies:

  • Palmaris brevis
  • Skin of the medial one and a half digits

Deep branch supplies:

  • All four palmar interossei (finger adduction)
  • All four dorsal interossei (finger abduction)
  • Three hypothenar muscles
  • Medial two lumbricals
  • Adductor pollicis

Because the palmar interossei are responsible for adduction at the metacarpophalangeal joints, they are the muscles being specifically tested during the paper-holding test.

Median Nerve (Option A): Controls thenar muscles and lateral lumbricals; not responsible for finger adduction.

Radial Nerve (Option C): Supplies extensors of wrist and fingers; no role in intrinsic hand muscle actions.

Posterior interosseous Nerve (Option D): Purely motor branch of radial nerve to forearm extensors; does not innervate hand muscles.

question_text: Which muscle is last muscle to be supplied by Radial nerve ?
explanation:
Radial nerve gives out muscular branches to supply the long head, medial head, and lateral head of triceps brachii muscles before and during its course in the radial sulcus. After it emerges out from the radial sulcus, it supplies the brachialis, brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus.

question_text: A patient reports abnormal sensations in the little finger and part of the ring finger, along with hand weakness and loss of finger coordination. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ulnar nerve supplies nearly all the intrinsic muscles of the hand, except the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals. It also provides cutaneous innervation to the medial 1½ fingers (little finger and medial half of the ring finger).

Therefore, the presence of abnormal sensations in these fingers, accompanied by hand weakness, points to ulnar nerve injury.

Effects of Ulnar Nerve Damage

  • Flexor weakness:
    • Difficulty flexing the 4th and 5th fingers due to paralysis of the medial part of flexor digitorum profundus and the 3rd and 4th lumbricals.
  • Thumb movement defect:
    • Inability to adduct the thumb because of paralysis of the adductor pollicis.

Motor Supply of the Ulnar Nerve (C7, C8, T1)


Explanation of other options:

Radial nerve (Option B): Injury causes wrist drop, not sensory loss in the little and ring fingers.

Median nerve (Option C): Innervates the thenar muscles and supplies sensation to the thumb, index, middle finger, and lateral half of the ring finger.

Axillary nerve (Option D): Supplies the deltoid muscle and skin over the shoulder; not related to hand symptoms.

question_text: Which functional deficit occurs following injury to the posterior interosseous nerve?
explanation:
Explanation:

The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is a motor branch of the radial nerve, arising after the radial nerve passes through the supinator muscle. It innervates most of the forearm extensor muscles, except brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL), and anconeus. Injury to the PIN leads to inability to extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, while wrist extension is relatively preserved due to intact ECRL. The PIN is purely motor, so sensory function remains unaffected.

Posterior Interosseous Nerve Palsy:

Explanation of other options:

Loss of extension of wrist (Option B): Incorrect because wrist extension is partially preserved due to the functional ECRL.

Loss of supination (Option C): Incorrect because supination is mainly performed by the biceps brachii, with minor contribution from the supinator (still partially functional).

Wrist drop (Option D): Incorrect because wrist drop occurs in proximal radial nerve injury, affecting all wrist and finger extensors; PIN injury primarily affects finger extension only.

question_text: A patient with leprosy presented with the deformity as shown below. Which nerve injury causes the given condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a claw hand deformity, which occurs due to ulnar nerve injury.

Ulnar Claw Hand

  • This deformity results from the imbalance of muscle action when the ulnar nerve is damaged.
  • There occurs paralysis of the lumbricals of the 4th and 5th fingers which is involved in the flexion at the MCP joints and extend the IP joints.
  • Loss of this action causes the MCP joints to become hyperextended and the IP joints to remain flexed, producing a claw-like appearance.
  • MCP joint hyperextension: This occurs in the ring and little fingers due to the unopposed action of the extensor digitorum muscles in the forearm.
  • PIP and DIP joint flexion: This occurs in the ring and little fingers due to the unopposed action of the flexor digitorum profundus muscle (specifically the medial half supplied by the ulnar nerve) and the flexor digitorum superficialis.
  • The index and middle fingers are often less affected because the lateral half of the FDP (which flexes these fingers at the DIP joint) and their lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve.

Common Causes

  • Leprosy,
  • Trauma at the elbow (cubital tunnel)
  • Wrist (Guyon's canal)

Tests for Ulnar Nerve

  • Froment's sign
    • The patient is asked to grip a sheet of paper forcefully between thumbs and index fingers while the examiner tries to pull it away; powerful flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint signals weakness of adductor pollicis and first dorsal interosseous with overcompensation by the flexor pollicis longus.

Treatment

  • Physiotherapy
  • Nerve grafting
  • Claw correction surgery

Explanation of other options:

Radial nerve (Option B): Radial nerve injury causes weakness of the wrist and finger extensors, leading to wrist drop,

Median nerve (Option C): Median nerve injury leads to weakness of the thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals, causing difficulty in thumb opposition, flexion of the index and middle fingers, producing the characteristic benediction sign.

Posterior interosseous nerve (Option D): Posterior interosseous nerve injury affects finger extension, leading to finger drop, not claw hand.

question_text: Supination of the hand and forearm would be diminished by loss of radial nerve function. But one very powerful supinator would remain intact and unaffected, namely:
explanation:
Biceps brachii supinates the arm, but it is not innervated by the radial nerve, instead, it is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve. So, it would not be affected by a radial nerve injury. Brachialis is also innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve, but it is only involved with flexing the forearm it is not a supinator. Brachioradialis flexes the elbow and assists in pronation and supination, it is innervated by the radial nerve and would be paralyzed after a radial nerve injury. Flexor carpi radialis is a flexor, not a supinator, it is innervated by the median nerve. Finally, supinator is innervated by the deep radial nerve.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 747

question_text: "Pronator teres syndrome" is a condition in which one of the following nerves is excessively compressed where it passes between the two heads of the pronator teres muscle. Which of the following nerves is entrapped?
explanation:
Each of the five terminal branches of the brachial plexus (musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, radial, and axillary nerves) passes through a muscular or osseofascial tunnel at some point in its distribution, where it may be subject to entrapment in a tunnel syndrome. The pronator teres muscle arises via two heads, one from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the other from the coronoid process of the ulna, with a tendinous arch connecting them. The median nerve exits the cubital fossa and enters the forearm by passing between these heads, where it may be unduly compressed in a pronator teres syndrome. This condition would influence much of the median nerve territory in the forearm plus the entire median nerve territory in the hand.

Reference: Textbook of B. D. Chaurasia, Volume-1, 9th Edition, Page No - 119, 125

question_text: In the process of doing an axillary lymph node dissection in a 50 year-old patient, the surgery resident cleans the space between the pectoralis major and minor muscles, in an attempt to remove all of the lateral pectoral lymph nodes. Upon recovery it is noted that the patient's lower pectoralis major is paralyzed. The nerve most likely injured is the:
explanation:
Since the medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor to reach pectoralis major, it seems likely for this nerve to be injured from trauma to the space between pectoralis minor and major. Also, remember that the medial pectoral nerve innervates the inferior part of pectoralis major, while the lateral pectoral nerve innervates the superior part of pectoralis major.

The medial pectoral nerve innervates both pectoralis major and pectoralis minor, while the lateral pectoral nerve innervates pectoralis major only. These two nerves are named after their origin from two different cords of the brachial plexus. (This explains why their names and relative locations are reversed from what you might expect.) The thoracodorsal nerve (which is also derived from the brachial plexus) innervates latissimus dorsi, and is not involved with the pectoral muscles. The other two nerves, axillary and suprascapular, are also derived from the brachial plexus and will be studied along with the upper limb.

question_text: After being thrown from a motorcycle moving at high speed, a 16-year-old female was found to have a paralyzed right pectoralis major muscle. Which set of movements at the shoulder joint would be found greatly weakened?
explanation:
Pectoralis major flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the arm. It is innervated by the lateral and medial pectoral nerves, from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus.

question_text: Which of the following forearm muscles has dual innervation supplied by both the median nerve and the ulnar nerve?
explanation:
The radial half of flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the median nerve, while the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve also supplies flexor carpi ulnaris in the anterior forearm. (Remember the ulnar nerve is the 1 1/2 nerve it supplies 1 1/2 muscles in the anterior forearm, and it supplies cutaneous innervation to 1 1/2 fingers on the ulnar side of the hand!)

Flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor pollicis longus, and pronator quadratus are innervated by the median nerve.

question_text: If the medial epicondyle of the humerus is fractured and the nerve passing dorsal to it is injured, which muscle would be most affected?
explanation:
The nerve passing dorsal to the medial epicondyle of the humerus is the ulnar nerve. In the forearm, the ulnar nerve innervates flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar side of flexor digitorum profundus. So, flexor carpi ulnaris would be most affected if the ulnar nerve was disrupted. What other symptoms might you see? Paralysis of hand muscles (except for the thenar compartment and the first two lumbricals) and numbness over the ulnar 1.5 digits in the hand!

The extensor muscles (extensor digitorum and extensor carpi ulnaris) are in the posterior compartment of the forearm, they are innervated by the radial nerve. Flexor digitorum superficialis is innervated by the median nerve only. Although the ulnar side of flexor digitorum profundus would be impaired following the injury, the radial side of flexor digitorum profundus would still be innervated by the median nerve.

question_text: Which of the following statements is not an anatomical event occurring at the level of insertion of the coracobrachialis?

question_text: During insertion of an IV cannula in the median cubital vein, the patient suddenly lost feeling on the radial side of the forearm. What nerve was injured?
explanation:
There are 3 nerves that might be damaged due to a venipuncture in the median cubital fossa. If the needle goes a bit lateral, the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve might be injured. This nerve is a branch of the musculocutaneous nerve which supplies the skin of the lateral side of the forearm. The patient's symptoms (loss of feeling on the radial side of the forearm) match with an injury to the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. If the needle goes a bit medial, it could injure the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve. This nerve is a direct branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus, it innervates skin on the medial side of the forearm. If the needle goes too deep, the median nerve might be injured. This would cause the patient to lose sensation on the palmar side of the lateral 3.5 digits.

The posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve is a branch of the radial nerve which supplies the posterior forearm. The superficial radial nerve is a terminal branch of the radial nerve which supplies the dorsum of the hand and the dorsal side of the lateral 2.5 digits. Neither of these nerves would be affected by a venipuncture in the median cubital fossa!

question_text: While riding a bike, a patient fell against a tree and fractured the shaft of the humerus at midlength. What nerve may be injured because of its close proximity to the injury?
explanation:
The radial nerve and the deep brachial vessels spiral around the shaft of the humerus in the radial groove. If the humerus is fractured, the radial nerve and the deep brachial vessels may be injured, since these structures are closely associated with the shaft of the humerus. The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus a fracture to this epicondyle may injure the ulnar nerve. The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical head of the humerus a fracture near the surgical head may endanger the axillary nerve. The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the median nerve travel superficially with the basilic vein and the brachial artery in a neurovascular bundle. These nerves are not going to be injured by a fracture of the humerus.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 818

question_text: During an industrial accident, a sheet metal worker lacerates the anterior surface of his wrist at the junction of his wrist and hand. Examination reveals no loss of hand function, but the skin on the thumb side of his palm is numb. Branches of which nerve must have been severed?
explanation:

The location of the injury also implies that there has been an injury to the median nerve, this nerve enters the hand by crossing under the flexor retinaculum on the anterior side of the wrist.

The lateral and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves provide cutaneous innervation to the anterior side of the forearm, the symptoms here are not consistent with an injury to these nerves. The radial nerve innervates the radial side of the dorsum of the hand but does not innervate the palmar side of the hand. The ulnar nerve innervates the medial (ulnar) side of both the dorsum and palm of the hand.

question_text: A road traffic accident patient has presented with features of a nerve injury involving the right upper limb. On examination, the patient is able to carry out flexion at the metacarpo-phalangeal (MCP) joint and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joint. The most likely nerve involved is?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The findings indicate an injury to the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), a deep branch of the radial nerve.
  • The lumbricals and interossei (supplied by median & ulnar nerves) flex MCP and extend IP joints → intact here.
  • The loss is specifically in MCP joint extension (finger drop), while wrist extension is preserved (because extensor carpi radialis longus & brevis are supplied by radial nerve before it gives off PIN).
  • PIN is a purely motor nerve → no sensory deficit is seen.
  • Common cause: Monteggia fracture-dislocation and iatrogenic injury during forearm surgeries.

Explanation of Other Options:

question_text: The patient who visited the outpatient department (OPD) displayed an irregular way of walking. During the examination, it was noticed that when the patient was instructed to balance on their left foot, there was a drop in their right hip. Which muscles are affected by paralysis in this particular patient?
option_a: Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
option_b: Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
option_c: Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The gluteus medius and gluteus minimus of the left side are the key pelvic stabilizers during single-leg stance on the left limb.
  • If these muscles are weakened or paralyzed, they fail to maintain the pelvis level, causing the contralateral hip (right side) to drop when the patient stands on the left leg.
  • This clinical finding is termed a positive Trendelenburg sign.

Trendelenburg sign:

  • Normally, when standing on one leg, the abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) on the stance side contract to keep the pelvis level or slightly elevated on the opposite side.
  • Paralysis of these muscles leads to a pelvic tilt toward the unsupported side (right side here), called an uncompensated Trendelenburg sign.
  • In walking, the patient may compensate by leaning the trunk toward the affected side (compensated Trendelenburg gait).
  • Bilateral involvement produces a waddling or "duck-like" gait.

Explanation of other options:

Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius (Option A): Their paralysis would affect hip extension and abduction on the right side but would not explain a right-sided hip drop while standing on the left foot.

Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus (Option B): Paralysis here would impair right hip abduction and pelvic stability when standing on the right foot, but not during stance on the left.

Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius (Option C): Loss of hip extension (gluteus maximus) and some abduction (gluteus medius) occurs, but the hip drop described is specifically due to loss of left gluteus medius and minimus, not maximus.

The Trendelenburg sign manifests as contralateral pelvic tilting when the patient attempts to balance on the affected limb, indicating weakness or dysfunction of the hip abductor mechanism.
  • This abnormal finding points to superior gluteal nerve pathology, resulting in an altered gait pattern where the patient demonstrates a characteristic lateral trunk lean toward the affected side during ambulation to compensate for the weakened abductor muscles.

Gluteus maximus (Option B): Extends and laterally rotates the thigh; innervated by inferior gluteal nerve. Weakness causes difficulty rising from a seated position or climbing stairs, not Trendelenburg gait.

Piriformis (Option C): Laterally rotates and abducts the thigh; innervated by nerve to piriformis. Weakness rarely causes gait abnormalities; more clinically significant for sciatic nerve compression.

Obturator internus (Option D): Laterally rotates the thigh; innervated by nerve to obturator internus. Weakness does not produce Trendelenburg sign.

question_text: If the second part of the axillary artery was interrupted, collateral blood flow could pass from branches of the thyrocervical trunk into which artery?
explanation:
One branch of the thyrocervical trunk is the suprascapular artery. This artery contributes to the scapular anastamosis with the dorsal scapular artery and the circumflex scapular artery. The circumflex scapular artery is a branch of the subscapular artery, which comes from the third part of the axillary artery. So, blood could flow from the suprascapular artery, through the scapular anastamosis, into the circumflex scapular artery, travel retrograde through the circumflex scapular artery and the subscapular artery, and reach the third part of the axillary artery. This would bypass any problems in the second part of the axillary artery. See Netter Plate 410B for a picture of this.

The anterior and posterior humeral circumflex arteries are both branches of the third part of the axillary artery. These two arteries anastomose with each other. They would not help shunt blood from the first to the third part of the axillary artery. The deep brachial artery is a branch of the brachial artery found in the deep arm. The thoracoacromial artery is a branch of the second part of the axillary artery. None of these other arteries would help shunt blood over an interruption in the second part of the axillary artery.

question_text: An open arterial anastomosis in the shoulder occurs between the suprascapular artery and which other artery?
explanation:
The circumflex scapular artery, the dorsal scapular artery, and the suprascapular artery create arterial anastomoses around the scapula. This means that the scapula will be supplied with blood even if one of these arteries is ligated. Additionally, if the subclavian or axillary artery needs to be ligated, blood can flow from the dorsal scapular artery and suprascapular artery to the circumflex scapular artery. This effectively shunts blood from the first part of the subclavian artery to the third part of the axillary artery so that the upper limb will still receive blood. The connection between the suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries is termed an open anastomosis because it is grossly visible, compared to the anastomosis with the dorsal scapular, which typically happens within small vessels.

The anterior circumflex humeral artery supplies the deltoid muscle. It originates from the third part of the axillary artery and anastomoses with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. The thoracodorsal artery is a branch of the subscapular artery that supplies latissimus dorsi. The transverse cervical artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk that occasionally gives rise to the dorsal scapular artery. None of these arteries contribute to the scapular anastomoses.

question_text: A patient with severe upper limb trauma requires surgical arterial ligation. The best chance of preserving collateral circulation to the forearm stump occurs when the ligature is placed at which level?

explanation:
The brachial artery bifurcates near the elbow. It forms two branches that become the radial and ulnar arteries. If these arteries were ligated after this bifurcation, there would be a chance at saving collateral circulation to the forearm because the ulnar artery might have already given off its common interosseous branch, which could carry blood to the forearm through the anterior and posterior interosseus arteries. Ligating near the beginning of the brachial artery would stop blood from flowing through the rest of the upper limb. Ligating near the origin of the deep artery, by the origin of the superior ulnar collateral artery, or near the origin of the inferior ulnar collateral artery might preserve enough collateral circulation to supply the elbow. However, there would not be collateral circulation to the forearm.

question_text: It was noted that after the injury the patient's face on the right side was flushed due to dilation of the blood vessels. The lack of vasoconstriction was due to interruption of what fibers somewhere along their course?

The radial artery runs on the radial side of the wrist, lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis. So, the radial pulse will be felt immediately lateral to this tendon. Remember the radial artery enters the wrist on the anterior side. This means that the extensor tendons, which are on the posterior side of the wrist, will not be involved with the radial artery! The tendons for flexor digitorum profundus and superficialis are found more towards the center of the wrist, not on the wrist's lateral side. These tendons cross under the flexor retinaculum to reach the hand.

question_text: The left brachiocephalic vein is derived from:
option_c: A shunt between left and right posterior cardinal veins
explanation:
The cranial end of left brachiocephalic vein is from left anterior cardinal, but the lower part develops as a shunt between left and right anterior cardinal veins. On the right side, the upper part of superior vena cava is from right anterior cardinal, while the lower part is old right common cardinal vein.

question_text: Which terminal branch of internal maxillary artery is responsible for posterior epistaxis?
explanation:
The sphenopalatine artery carries the most significant volume of blood to the nose and is the source of most posteriorly based nose bleeds. Epistaxis caused by posterior bleeding accounts for 10% of cases, with 80% of bleeding coming from the sphenopalatine artery. Posterior epistaxis is most often associated with atherosclerotic disease, hypertension, and diabetes, but can occur iatrogenically or from idiopathic causes. Posterior bleeding may remain asymptomatic or may present insidiously as hematemesis, anemia, or melena. Additional clinical presentations of posterior epistaxis include the presence of blood in oropharynx; a history of recurrent epistaxis; failure to control epistaxis by nasal packing; the presence of clots in the area of sphenopalatine foramen; the presence of clots in maxillary sinus ostium; and absence of bleeding areas in the anterior nasal septum.
